o: How to apply to God under troubles, and how to behave in prosperous and in adverse circumstances.
To look upon all evil as proceeding from ourselves, and all good from God.
The duty of watching against a rash temper, and of receiving the word of God with meekness.
The difference between vain pretences and real religion.
bg: (1.) Author of, was James the Less, the Lord's brother, one of the twelve apostles. He was one of the three pillars of the Church (Gal. 2:9).
ch.s: This chapter covers: How to apply to God under troubles, and how to behave in prosperous and in adverse circumstances (vv. 1–11); To look upon all evil as proceeding from ourselves, and all good from God (vv. 12–18); The duty of watching against a rash temper, and of receiving the word of God with meekness (vv. 19–21); And of living according thereto (vv. 22–25); The difference between vain pretences and real religion (vv. 26,27). People named: James.
ch.mh: Christianity teaches men to be joyful under troubles: such exercises are sent from God's love; and trials in the way of duty will brighten our graces now, and our crown at last.
q: Read verses 1–11 (How to apply to God under troubles, and how to behave in prosperous and in adverse circumstances). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 12–18 (To look upon all evil as proceeding from ourselves, and all good from God), what do you learn about suffering and endurance?
Verse 12 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside 1 Peter 5:10. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does James’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of sin and repentance in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of James?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: And let us remember, that nothing avails in Christ Jesus, but faith that worketh by love, purifies the heart, subdues carnal lusts, and obeys God's commands.
ch.a: Bring a present hardship to God and memorize the key verse as an anchor.

o: All professions of faith are vain, if not producing love and justice to others.
The necessity of good works to prove the sincerity of faith, which otherwise will be of no more advantage than the faith of devils.
bg: (1.) Author of, was James the Less, the Lord's brother, one of the twelve apostles. He was one of the three pillars of the Church (Gal. 2:9).

The history of Abraham made a wide and deep impression on the ancient world, and references to it are interwoven in the religious traditions of almost all Eastern nations. He is called "the friend of God" (James 2:23), "faithful Abraham" (Gal. 3:9), "the father of us all" (Rom. 4:16).

In the New Testament reference is made to his having been "offered up" by his father (Heb. 11:17; James 2:21), and to his blessing his sons (Heb. 11:20). As the child of promise, he is contrasted with Ishmael (Rom. 9:7, 10; Gal. 4:28; Heb. 11:18).
ch.s: This chapter covers: All professions of faith are vain, if not producing love and justice to others (vv. 1–13); The necessity of good works to prove the sincerity of faith, which otherwise will be of no more advantage than the faith of devils (vv. 14–26). People named: Abraham, Isaac, Rahab.
ch.mh: Those who profess faith in Christ as the Lord of glory, must not respect persons on account of mere outward circumstances and appearances, in a manner not agreeing with their profession of being disciples of the lowly Jesus.
q: Read verses 1–13 (All professions of faith are vain, if not producing love and justice to others). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 14–26 (The necessity of good works to prove the sincerity of faith, which otherwise will be of no more advantage than the faith of devils), what do you learn about faith and trust?
Verse 5 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Matthew 5:3. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Abraham’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of law and instruction in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of James?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: This is the grace of God wherein we stand, and we should stand to it.
ch.a: Name one worry and deliberately hand it over to God in prayer each day this week.

o: Cautions against proud behaviour, and the mischief of an unruly tongue.
The excellence of heavenly wisdom, in opposition to that which is worldly.
bg: (1.) Author of, was James the Less, the Lord's brother, one of the twelve apostles. He was one of the three pillars of the Church (Gal. 2:9).
ch.s: This chapter covers: Cautions against proud behaviour, and the mischief of an unruly tongue (vv. 1–12); The excellence of heavenly wisdom, in opposition to that which is worldly (vv. 13–18).
ch.mh: We are taught to dread an unruly tongue, as one of the greatest evils.
q: Read verses 1–12 (Cautions against proud behaviour, and the mischief of an unruly tongue). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 13–18 (The excellence of heavenly wisdom, in opposition to that which is worldly), what do you learn about wisdom?
Verse 17 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Galatians 5:22–23. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
Where do you see the theme of peace in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of James?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: Then, depending on Divine grace, let us take heed to bless and curse not; and let us aim to be consistent in our words and actions.
ch.a: Before a decision this week, pause and ask what this chapter would counsel.

o: Here are cautions against corrupt affections, and love of this world, which is enmity to God.
Exhortations to undertake no affairs of life, without constant regard to the will and providence of God.
bg: (1.) Author of, was James the Less, the Lord's brother, one of the twelve apostles. He was one of the three pillars of the Church (Gal. 2:9).
ch.s: This chapter covers: Here are cautions against corrupt affections, and love of this world, which is enmity to God (vv. 1–10); Exhortations to undertake no affairs of life, without constant regard to the will and providence of God (vv. 11–17).
ch.mh: Since all wars and fightings come from the corruptions of our own hearts, it is right to mortify those lusts that war in the members.
q: Read verses 1–10 (Here are cautions against corrupt affections, and love of this world, which is enmity to God). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 11–17 (Exhortations to undertake no affairs of life, without constant regard to the will and providence of God), what do you learn about law and instruction?
Verse 8 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Psalms 145:18. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
Where do you see the theme of war and conflict in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of James?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: We have the law of God, which is a rule to all; let us not presume to set up our own notions and opinions as a rule to those about us, and let us be careful that we be not condemned of the Lord.
ch.a: Show the same mercy you have received to someone who does not deserve it.

o: The judgments of God denounced against rich unbelievers.
Exhortation to patience and meekness under tribulations.
Cautions against rash swearing Prayer recommended in afflictive and prosperous circumstances, Christians to confess their faults to each other.
The happiness of being the means of the conversion of a sinner.
bg: (1.) Author of, was James the Less, the Lord's brother, one of the twelve apostles. He was one of the three pillars of the Church (Gal. 2:9).

Persecuted, an Arabian patriarch who resided in the land of Uz (q.v.). While living in the midst of great prosperity, he was suddenly overwhelmed by a series of sore trials that fell upon him. Amid all his sufferings he maintained his integrity.
ch.s: This chapter covers: The judgments of God denounced against rich unbelievers (vv. 1–6); Exhortation to patience and meekness under tribulations (vv. 7–11); Cautions against rash swearing Prayer recommended in afflictive and prosperous circumstances, Christians to confess their faults to each other (vv. 12–18); The happiness of being the means of the conversion of a sinner (vv. 19,20). People named: Job, Elias.
ch.mh: Public troubles are most grievous to those who live in pleasure, and are secure and sensual, though all ranks suffer deeply at such times.
q: Read verses 1–6 (The judgments of God denounced against rich unbelievers). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 7–11 (Exhortation to patience and meekness under tribulations), what do you learn about prayer?
Verse 16 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Jeremiah 29:12–13. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Job’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of suffering and endurance in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of James?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: Let us in our several stations keep these things in mind, sparing no pains in God's service, and the event will prove that our labour is not in vain in the Lord.
ch.a: Set aside a specific time this week to pray through this chapter's key verse.
